source_text:
The time was the beginning of the morning,
And up the sun was mounting with those stars
That with him were, what time the Love Divine

At first in motion set those beauteous things;
So were to me occasion of good hope,
The variegated skin of that wild beast,

The hour of time, and the delicious season;
But not so much, that did not give me fear
A lion’s aspect which appeared to me.
modern_text:
It was the break of dawn, and the sun was rising with those same stars that accompanied it when divine Love first set all beautiful things in motion.

The early hour and the sweet season gave me reason to hope, despite the beast's dappled hide.

But that hope was short-lived, for a lion appeared before me.

As much time as passes between the close of the third hour and sunrise — that much appeared to remain of the sun's course before nightfall.

It was evening there and midnight here.

source_text:
Of every malice that wins hate in Heaven,
Injury is the end; and all such end
Either by force or fraud afflicteth others.

But because fraud is man’s peculiar vice,
More it displeases God; and so stand lowest
The fraudulent, and greater dole assails them.

All the first circle of the Violent is;
But since force may be used against three persons,
In three rounds ’tis divided and constructed.

To God, to ourselves, and to our neighbour can we
Use force; I say on them and on their things,
As thou shalt hear with reason manifest.
modern_text:
The aim of every malice that earns the hatred of Heaven is to cause injury, and every such aim afflicts others through either force or fraud.

But because fraud is a sin unique to humans, it offends God more. Therefore the fraudulent are placed lowest, and greater suffering assails them.

The entire first of the three circles holds the violent. But since violence can be directed against three targets, it is divided into three rings.

Against God, against oneself, and against one's neighbor — violence can be done to any of these, as you will hear with clear reasoning.

source_text:
As the geometrician, who endeavours
To square the circle, and discovers not,
By taking thought, the principle he wants,

Even such was I at that new apparition;
I wished to see how the image to the circle
Conformed itself, and how it there finds place;

But my own wings were not enough for this,
Had it not been that then my mind there smote
A flash of lightning, wherein came its wish.

Here vigour failed the lofty fantasy:
But now was turning my desire and will,
Even as a wheel that equally is moved,

The Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
modern_text:
Like the geometer who sets himself to square the circle and cannot find, no matter how he thinks, the principle he needs,

Such was I before that new sight. I wished to see how the image conformed to the circle and how it found its place there.

But my own wings were not enough for that — except that my mind was struck by a flash of lightning in which its wish came true.

Here power failed the lofty imagination. But already my desire and my will were being turned, like a wheel that is moved evenly,

By the Love that moves the sun and the other stars.
